assessmentSummary.identity: A live-partner choice-reaction task in which a point to left, right, or forward selects the sprint direction after the athlete is set.
currentCardFindings: The description identifies three directions but not partner position, point visibility, start stance, wait interval, target angles, distances, first-step or turn rule, direction balance, finish, or run-out.
This is not a simple sprint-start reaction because the cue selects among multiple movement paths.
Existing legacy links are broad reactive drills; exact-title partner-point media found by visible search still require full review.

proposedDosage.progressWhen: correct choices, balanced direction quality, speed, braking, and run-out remain repeatable

coachCues: Own the first step and finish

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Retain as a distinct reactive-agility definition because the live point selects among three directions. Do not merge with simple auditory or one-light forward sprint starts.

currentCardSnapshot.description: The athlete waits for a live cue (partner points left, right, or forward), selects the correct answer, performs the movement response, and resets before the next rep. The rep counts only when the athlete reacts to the real stimulus rather than guessing early.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint starts and the minimum auditory reaction time
claims: An auditory sprint start includes a measurable interval between an unpredictable go-signal and force or movement onset.

Partner Point Reactive Sprint Start must define cue modality, cue meaning, waiting interval, allowed response choices, start stance, false-start rule, direction, sprint distance, finish, and run-out. Simple go reaction and directional choice reaction are not interchangeable.

evidence.sourceTitle: Are Change of Direction Speed and Reactive Agility Useful for Determining the Optimal Field Position for Young Soccer Players?
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
claims: A visually cued reactive task differs from a pre-planned task because the athlete must identify an unpredictable illuminated target before selecting the direction.

Partner Point Reactive Sprint Start belongs either to a simple externally cued sprint-start variant or to reactive agility with perceptual decision and direction selection; the exact cue-response mapping determines which.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint Acceleration Mechanics: The Major Role of Hamstrings in Horizontal Force Production
claims: Sprint acceleration requires coordinated hip, knee, and ankle action, including hamstring contribution to horizontal force production.

Represent visual or auditory processing and head-eye orientation as task demands, then gluteal, hamstring, quadriceps, hip-flexor, plantar-flexor, foot, trunk, and reciprocal arm roles; add braking and lateral control for directional choices.

evidence.sourceTitle: Biomechanical Performance Factors in the Track and Field Sprint Start: A Systematic Review
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
claims: Early sprint acceleration is associated with forward-directed impulse, propulsive force, and progressive projection.

The prepared response should preserve a repeatable start and first steps. Directional-choice responses additionally require head-eye pickup, safe reorientation, braking or turning mechanics, and a clear target path.

evidence.sourceTitle: Sprint starts and the minimum auditory reaction time
claims: Auditory reaction time includes neural and neuromuscular components in addition to physical sprint-start execution.

Score technical complexity, absolute-load demand, coordination, supervision, failure consequence, impact, work-capacity demand, and overall difficulty directly; athlete experience is programming context and never an exercise-card skill level.

evidence.sourceTitle: Correlations between muscle-tendon parameters and acceleration ability in 20 m sprints
claims: Power output is highest during the first acceleration steps.

Partner Point Reactive Sprint Start must track attempts, accepted versus anticipated responses, decision errors, distance, sprint and braking contacts, stance and direction distribution, surface, posterior-chain and plantar-flexor stress, technical or perceptual fatigue, recovery, and total session volume.
Quality sprint work requires a suitable surface, target, spacing, run-out, and recovery.

Require a clear dry lane or direction grid, unobstructed sight or hearing, consistent non-startling cue delivery, athlete separation, safe targets and run-outs, and any light, whistle, cone, or timing equipment specified by the variant.
Acceleration work should prescribe distance, intensity, repetitions, sets, and recovery.

Use two to six quality reactions per cue or direction with randomized waits and roughly 60–180 seconds recovery for high-intent sprint starts; directional tasks must balance choices and record correct responses separately from movement time.

evidence.sourceTitle: Are Change of Direction Speed and Reactive Agility Useful for Determining the Optimal Field Position for Young Soccer Players?
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
claims: Reactive trials require the athlete to identify the presented target rather than execute a known direction.
Set the stance, focus on the defined cue source, wait without guessing, execute only the mapped response, accelerate through the target, and use the assigned deceleration or run-out path.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Training should use appropriate supervision, correct technique, manageable demands, and gradual progression.

Stop for pain, startle or distress, missed or ambiguous cue, repeated anticipation, slip, stumble, lane conflict, unsafe turn or brake, marked decision or speed decline, or inability to complete the run-out safely.
Acceleration and maximal-velocity sprinting are distinct qualities, and high-quality sprint work should not become dense conditioning.

Partner Point Reactive Sprint Start belongs after preparation and before fatigue. Program simple reaction before multiple-choice direction tasks, and separate reaction accuracy from sprint or agility output when reviewing performance.
Acceleration develops across successive steps rather than through immediate upright running.
Show the exact stance, cue device and location, allowed mappings, one accepted and one false-start example, all target directions, finish and run-out paths, and a pre-planned regression.

evidence.sourceTitle: Are Change of Direction Speed and Reactive Agility Useful for Determining the Optimal Field Position for Young Soccer Players?
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
claims: Reactive assessment separates the unplanned visual-target condition from the same pre-planned movement path.

Provide a randomized cue schedule, cue and movement timestamps when measured, response accuracy, anticipation and no-response rules, stance and direction balance, lane control, technique and speed stops, and exact simple-versus-choice classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Training and Long-Term Athletic Development
claims: Speed training should be developmentally appropriate and based on movement competency.

Accessibility options include a comfortable stance, one cue modality, one known response, longer wait window, submaximal intent, shorter distance, high-contrast visual target, non-startling sound, demonstration, fewer choices, fewer reps, and longer recovery.

evidence.sourceTitle: Are Change of Direction Speed and Reactive Agility Useful for Determining the Optimal Field Position for Young Soccer Players?

claims: Pre-planned and reactive direction tasks use similar paths but differ in whether the target direction is known.

Whistle, clap, and verbal go can be aliases of one simple auditory signal; changing cue modality is a variant, while adding multiple response choices, a live opponent, a ball, or a required direction change may require a distinct definition.
